title: Anchors & Concept Stacking
description: Enforce structural position boundaries (^, $, \b) combined with M1 classes and M2 quantifiers.

primer.definition: ^ asserts the start of a string or line, $ asserts the end of a string or line, and \b asserts a word boundary position.
primer.goldenRule: Anchors do not consume any characters—they strictly enforce location boundaries.
primer.mentalModel: Think of anchors as zero-width invisible position checkpoints. They evaluate where a match occurs within the text rather than matching actual visible characters.
points: ^ enforces matching strictly from the beginning of the input string.
$ enforces matching strictly up to the end of the input string.
\b matches the zero-width boundary position between a word character (\w) and a non-word character (\W) or string edge.
Wrapping a pattern with \b on both sides (e.g., \bcat\b) enforces whole-word matching, preventing partial matches inside longer words.
Wrapping patterns in ^ and $ (^...$) converts partial substring matching into exact full-string validation.
pitfalls: Confusing word boundaries (\b) with whitespace (\s): \b is a zero-width assertion that consumes no characters, whereas \s matches actual space/tab characters.
Omitting ^ or $ during input validation: an unanchored pattern like \d+ will match digits inside 'abc123xyz' instead of enforcing a digit-only string.
Placing ^ inside character sets ([^...]): inside square brackets, ^ negates the set rather than matching the start of the string.
